Think nuclear engineering is just about power plants? Think again!
From fusion energy and plasma physics to space exploration and advanced technology, nuclear engineering offers exciting opportunities to tackle some of the world's biggest challenges.
In this episode of Exploring Engineering at UC Berkeley, undergraduate students Conrad Buck and Isaac Duarte Valdez share their unexpected journeys into nuclear engineering. entry.title: Virtual simulation of the 7.9M 1906 San Francisco earthquake spotlights human behavioral response

media:group.media:title: Virtual simulation of the 7.9M 1906 San Francisco earthquake spotlights human behavioral response
media:group.media:description: UC Berkeley researchers are seeking to better understand people’s earthquake risk perception with the goal of improving earthquake safety. They recently set out to create an immersive representation of an indoor earthquake by synchronizing the shaking of the Shake House (https://www.calacademy.org/exhibits/california-state-of-nature/shake-house), an earthquake simulator at the California Academy of Sciences, with a virtual reality environment they developed. So when test subjects saw things falling in virtual reality, the physics corresponded to the shaking they felt. During the experiment, test subjects wore VR headsets that recorded their gaze, and they could press a button on the VR controller whenever they felt at risk of being injured. “For earthquake engineers, this gives us a new way to go beyond computational models and study how people perceive risk and make decisions as earthquakes unfold,” said civil engineering professor Luis Ceferino. “Getting answers would give us more information to develop policy, recommendations and guidance for what to do when there is an earthquake to further reduce people’s risk of injury.” (Video courtesy the researchers)

entry.title: UC Berkeley Ph.D. Student Combats Foodborne Illness with Electronic Nose

media:group.media:title: UC Berkeley Ph.D. Student Combats Foodborne Illness with Electronic Nose
media:group.media:description:
How to win first place at UC Berkeley’s Grad Slam? Follow your next-gen electronic nose.
At least that’s what worked for Carla Bassil, a Ph.D. student in electrical engineering and computer sciences.
She is working to improve food safety, one gas sensor chip at a time.
This multi-modal gas sensing technology could sniff out spoilage, contamination and unsafe compounds in our food — long before our human noses could detect any defects.
It’s an engineering feat that could prevent the food-borne illnesses that result in 128,000 hospitalizations and 3,000 deaths in America each year.
